title: Signal or 'Noise': Human Reactions to Robot Errors in the Wild
authors: Maia Stiber,Sameer Khan,Russell Taylor,Chien-Ming Huang
abstract: In the real world, robots frequently make errors, yet little is known about people’s social responses to errors outside of lab settings. Prior work has shown that social signals are reliable and useful for error management in constrained interactions, but it is unclear if this holds in the real world—especially with a non-social robot in repeated and group interactions with successive or propagated errors. To explore this, we built a coffee robot and conducted a public field deployment (N=49N=49). We found that participants consistently expressed varied social signals in response to errors and other stimuli, particularly during group interactions. Our findings suggest that social signals in the wild are rich (with participants volunteering information about the interaction), but “noisy.” We discuss lessons, benefits, and challenges for using social signals in real-world HRI.
introduction:
In lab settings, social signals—verbal and nonverbal cues people naturally express during interaction—have been proven to be a good and reliable indicator of robot errors [6, 26, 44, 49]. Models of these signals, when integrated into larger robotic systems, enable flexible and automatic error detection [51]. However, this has been in the lab with single users and single interactions, though a few studies have begun exploring social robot interaction ruptures [44].

It is not evident how these signals manifest outside the lab with a non-social robot. Prior work has not examined responses to errors during group and repeated interactions in public spaces. Our questions are: (1) how do people react to robot errors in the wild?; (2) how do people react during interactions in the wild with a non-social robot across successive errors, repeated interactions, and in group interactions?; and (3) what opportunities and challenges arise for using social signals to manage errors in real-world systems?

To answer these questions, we conducted a three-week public field deployment. First, we developed an autonomous coffee robot field deployment and data collection system to (1) collect data, (2) autonomously provide a service that is commonly experienced in the real world, and (3) safely operate in the face of user interference and without experimenter supervision. Then, we ran the deployment and collected 39 interactions with 49 unique participants.

We found that individuals and groups responded socially to robot errors in the wild across repeated interactions (Fig. LABEL:fig:teaser), consistently displaying diverse verbal and non-verbal social signals. These were triggered not only by the robot and its errors (or absence of) but also by people, phones, and environmental factors. Group interactions produced more complex social signals, with a higher density of relevant and irrelevant (“noisy”) signals. Thus, social signals serve as a modality for participants to volunteer information about the interaction and reflect participants’ shifting mental models across multiple errors and interactions. title: InterPrior: Scaling Generative Control for Physics-Based Human-Object Interactions
authors: Sirui Xu,Samuel Schulter,Morteza Ziyadi,Xialin He,Xiaohan Fei,Yu-Xiong Wang,Liangyan Gui
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Graphics (cs.GR); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Humans rarely plan whole-body interactions with objects at the level of explicit whole-body movements. High-level intentions, such as affordance, define the goal, while coordinated balance, contact, and manipulation can emerge naturally from underlying physical and motor priors. Scaling such priors is key to enabling humanoids to compose and generalize loco-manipulation skills across diverse contexts while maintaining physically coherent whole-body coordination. To this end, we introduce InterPrior, a scalable framework that learns a unified generative controller through large-scale imitation pretraining and post-training by reinforcement learning. InterPrior first distills a full-reference imitation expert into a versatile, goal-conditioned variational policy that reconstructs motion from multimodal observations and high-level intent. While the distilled policy reconstructs training behaviors, it does not generalize reliably due to the vast configuration space of large-scale human-object interactions. To address this, we apply data augmentation with physical perturbations, and then perform reinforcement learning finetuning to improve competence on unseen goals and initializations. Together, these steps consolidate the reconstructed latent skills into a valid manifold, yielding a motion prior that generalizes beyond the training data, e.g., it can incorporate new behaviors such as interactions with unseen objects. We further demonstrate its effectiveness for user-interactive control and its potential for real robot deployment.
introduction:
Human-object interaction (HOI) is inherently hierarchical: humans plan at a high level with sparse intentions, while detailed limb coordination, balance, and contact emerge through fast, intuitive motor responses [62]. For instance, when reaching for a bottle, we plan the hand’s target and object motion, while the rest of the body follows through subconscious coordination.
Motion imitation policies [86] have scaled to large HOI skills but rely on explicit planners for dense full-body and object references. In contrast, an interaction motor prior should sample feasible loco-manipulation behaviors from a distribution conditioned on sparse goals, e.g., next-second hand contact, rather than simply mimicking deterministic, fully specified trajectories.

To model a distribution over feasible loco-manipulation behaviors, early work [15, 44] learns a generative controller via adversarial distributional matching and then uses reinforcement learning (RL) to promote task achievement under it. These methods can expand motion coverage beyond demonstrations, but are hard to scale due to unstable optimization, discriminator mode collapse, and handcrafted task objectives. An alternative is to distill reference imitation policies [35], with goal conditioning [58] achieved without task-specific design. While these approaches can absorb large-scale data, they can be brittle when reference coverage lags far behind the configuration space—as in loco-manipulation, where even a few object degrees of freedom can induce a combinatorial explosion of contact modes and relative poses with different geometries.

To address these limitations, we introduce InterPrior, a physics-based HOI controller that is scalable along four axes (Figure LABEL:fig:teaser). (I) task coverage: a single policy supports multiple goal formulations, e.g., sparse targets and their compositions; (II) skill coverage: the same training recipe scales to large HOI data and enables affordance-rich interactions beyond simple grasping; (III) motion coverage: it generates expressive trajectories instead of merely reconstructing demonstrations; and (IV) dynamics coverage: it maintains task success under varied physical properties.

Our key insight is that RL finetuning is essential for turning distillation from data reconstruction into a robust, generalizable policy. Distillation alone cannot cover the full HOI configuration space, yet RL applied in isolation often drifts toward unnatural reward-hacking behaviors. We therefore use distillation to provide a strong, natural initialization, and apply RL as a local optimizer that improves robustness while remaining anchored to the pretrained model.
Concretely, we leverage distillation to inherit broad skills from large-scale HOI demonstrations, by training a masked conditional variational policy to reconstruct motor control from sparse, multimodal goals, distilled from a reference imitation expert. We then RL finetune this policy to consolidate its latent skills into a valid interaction manifold. The finetuning optimizes two objectives: improving success on unseen goals and initializations, and preserving pretrained knowledge through regularization. It leverages the pretrained base policy to synthesize natural in-between motions, with failure states to acquire recovery behaviors, e.g. re-approach and re-grasp. Together, these steps transform reconstructed latent skills into a stable, continuous manifold that generalizes beyond the training trajectories.

Our contributions are fourfold. (I) We present InterPrior, a generalizable generative controller for physics-based human-object interaction, encompassing diverse skills rather than fixed procedural routines (e.g., approach, grasp, place) typical of prior work. (II) We develop an RL finetuning strategy that enables robust failure recovery and goal execution across varied configurations while maintaining human-like coordination. The resulting controller supports mid-trajectory command switching, re-grasps after failures, and remains stable under perturbations.
(III) We show that our finetuning strategy naturally extends to
novel objects and interactions, functioning as a reusable prior.
(IV) We demonstrate embodiment flexibility by training on the G1 humanoid [64] with sim-to-sim evaluation and enabling real-time control via keyboard interfaces.

title: Learning Event-Based Shooter Models from Virtual Reality Experiments
authors: Christopher A. McClurg,Alan R. Wagner
comment: Preprint under review for conference publication.
abstract: Virtual reality (VR) has emerged as a powerful tool for evaluating school security measures in high-risk scenarios such as school shootings, offering experimental control and high behavioral fidelity. However, assessing new interventions in VR requires recruiting new participant cohorts for each condition, making large-scale or iterative evaluation difficult. These limitations are especially restrictive when attempting to learn effective intervention strategies, which typically require many training episodes. To address this challenge, we develop a data-driven discrete-event simulator (DES) that models shooter movement and in-region actions as stochastic processes learned from participant behavior in VR studies. We use the simulator to examine the impact of a robot-based shooter intervention strategy. Once shown to reproduce key empirical patterns, the DES enables scalable evaluation and learning of intervention strategies that are infeasible to train directly with human subjects. Overall, this work demonstrates a high-to-mid fidelity simulation workflow that provides a scalable surrogate for developing and evaluating autonomous school-security interventions.
introduction:
School shootings remain a persistent and growing concern in the United States, as more than half (53.3%) of documented gun-related school incidents occurred within the past seven years [23]. Exposure to such events is associated with elevated rates of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and anxiety among students [29, 8]. Although numerous school-security measures have been implemented—ranging from hardened infrastructure to behavioral profiling—many lack empirical validation of their efficacy [1, 27, 15]. In addition, some measures have been linked to increased student anxiety, reduced trust, and erosion of school climate [4].

Evaluating school-security measures for school shootings is difficult, as the detailed behavioral data required for validation are limited and cannot be systematically collected from real events [7]. Although ecologically valid, unannounced experiments in real schools would pose unacceptable physical, ethical, and psychological risks [29, 8]. Virtual reality (VR) may offer a practical alternative, allowing participants to assume the role of a shooter in a simulated school environment while detailed behavior and physiological measurements are taken [18]. Prior work has demonstrated statistical equivalence between VR-generated behavior and real shooter data while also showing promise for evaluating intervention strategies [19].

Despite its advantages, conducting human-subject experiments in VR to evaluate school-security measures does not scale. Each change in experimental condition—whether testing a new intervention or refining an existing one—requires a separate human-subject study with a new participant cohort. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a discrete-event simulation (DES) as a scalable surrogate for conditional human-subject experiments, in which shooter behavior is modeled as a stochastic process learned from human-subject data in VR.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the relevant background. Section III describes the participant data collected in virtual reality that was used to construct and calibrate the simulator. Sections IV–V then describe and evaluate the fidelity of the discrete-event simulator. Section VI demonstrates the use of the simulator in a sample-intensive agent-learning task, which would otherwise be infeasible to carry out using a series of human-subject experiments.

abstract: The well-studied Dispersion problem is a fundamental coordination problem in distributed robotics, where a set of mobile robots must relocate so that each occupies a distinct node of a network. introduction:
The well-studied Dispersion problem, first proposed by Augustine and Moses Jr. [1], asks k≤nk\leq n mobile robots, initially placed on the nodes of an nn-node graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), to autonomously reposition so that each node contains at most one robot. In this paper, we introduce and study the Location-Aware Dispersion problem, a generalization of Dispersion that incorporates location-awareness.

Location-Aware Dispersion.
Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a connected, undirected, anonymous graph with nn nodes. Each node v∈Vv\in V has a color 𝖼𝗈𝗅​(v)∈𝒞={c1,…,ct}\mathsf{col}(v)\in\mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{t}\}, where multiple nodes may share a same color. A set ℛ={r1,…,rk}\mathcal{R}=\{r_{1},\dots,r_{k}\} of k≤nk\leq n mobile robots is given, with each robot ri∈ℛr_{i}\in\mathcal{R} having a color 𝖼𝗈𝗅​(ri)∈𝒞\mathsf{col}(r_{i})\in\mathcal{C}. Initially, robots are arbitrarily placed on GG. The goal is to relocate the robots so that each one occupies a distinct node matching its color, with no two robots sharing a node.

This variant models scenarios where robots must be assigned to category-specific tasks or resources. For example, in a multi-company charging infrastructure, nodes represent charging stations belonging to different providers, and robots (or electric vehicles) must be routed to stations of the corresponding provider. More generally, Location-Aware Dispersion captures coordination in logistics, transportation, and multi-robot systems, where robots are constrained by category-specific requirements. When |𝒞|=1|\mathcal{C}|=1, Location-Aware Dispersion reduces to Dispersion, as a robot can settle at any node as long as no other robot settles there.

The objective in Dispersion is to place the robots on distinct nodes; once a collision-free (dispersed) configuration is achieved, the problem is considered solved. In contrast, a dispersed configuration alone does not suffice for Location-Aware Dispersion, i.e., even when all robots occupy distinct nodes, the configuration may still be invalid if a robot is placed on a node whose color does not match its own. Therefore, for Location-Aware Dispersion, a dispersed configuration, which is a solution to Dispersion, is only a necessary condition, but not a sufficient one. Additionally, it has been shown that Dispersion is always solvable on any arbitrary nn-node graph for any number of robots k≤nk\leq n, without prior knowledge of kk or nn. In contrast, we will show that Location-Aware Dispersion is not always solvable. This means Location-Aware Dispersion is a more difficult problem than Dispersion. Consequently, Location-Aware Dispersion introduces additional challenges compared to Dispersion, since robots must not only avoid collisions but also respect color constraints. As in Dispersion, two complexity measures are central: time complexity, the number of rounds, and memory complexity, the amount of persistent memory per robot. The graph nodes are anonymous and memory-less. The objective is to design both time and memory efficient deterministic algorithms for Location-Aware Dispersion as well as establish impossibility and lower bounds, that characterize the minimal requirements for solving the problem.

We consider an undirected, unweighted graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) with n=|V|n=|V| nodes, m=|E|m=|E| edges. A node v∈Vv\in V is assigned a color cic_{i}, 𝒞={c1,c2,…,ct},t≤n,\mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},c_{2},...,c_{t}\},t\leq n, is the set of all colors used for the nodes. Each node v∈Vv\in V is memory-less, meaning it does not store any information. Each edge incident to a vv is labeled using the port number [1,δv][1,\delta_{v}], where δv\delta_{v} is the degree of node vv. Hence, an edge connecting two different vertices is assigned a port number at each end. There is no relation between the port labels at the two ends of an edge.

We consider k≤nk\leq n robots placed at the node of GG denoted by ℛ={r1,r2…..rk}\mathcal{R}=\{r_{1},r_{2}.....r_{k}\}. The initial arrangement of the robots on GG corresponds to: (i) the rooted configuration, where all k≤nk\leq n robots are collocated at a single source node; (ii) the dispersed configuration, where each node initially hosts at most one robot; and (iii) the general configuration, where the initial placement is neither rooted or dispersed. Each robot has a unique ID in the range [1,kO​(1)][1,k^{O(1)}]. If the robots are aware of the type of their initial configuration (rooted, dispersed, or general), the configuration is said to be known; otherwise, it is referred to as an unknown configuration.
A robot r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R} is assigned a color cic_{i}, where 𝒞={c1,c2,…,ct}\mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},c_{2},...,c_{t}\} is the set of all colors used for the robots, and t≤kt\leq k. Robots can move between vertices via edges; however, they can only occupy vertices and are not allowed to stay on edges.
We consider the local communication model (aka the face-2-face model), i.e.,
where the robots located at a node v∈Vv\in V can communicate and can share their data and ID with only the other collocated robots at vv.

Our main results on Location-Aware Dispersion are summarized in Table 1, while a comparison with the state-of-the-art results on Dispersion is provided in Table 2. We highlight that the lower bound for Location-Aware Dispersion is strictly higher than that for Dispersion, and moreover, Location-Aware Dispersion is impossible to solve when k=1k=1 and nn is unknown. This stands in contrast to Dispersion, which remains solvable under these conditions (see Section 2).

We first present a deterministic algorithm for the rooted configuration assuming prior knowledge of both nn and kk. We then extend our results to configurations that are known in advance, namely rooted, dispersed, and general configurations, considering both settings where nn and kk are known and where such knowledge is unavailable (Sections 3 to 6). Finally, in Section 7, we study scenarios in which the initial configuration is unknown. Taken together, these results provide a nearly tight
characterization of the complexity of Location-Aware Dispersion in anonymous port-labeled memory-less networks, establishing both its algorithmic feasibility and its fundamental limitations.

Dispersion is the most closely related problem to Location-Aware Dispersion. Dispersion was first introduced by Augustine and Moses Jr. in [1]. Later, the problem was studied in more detail for the case k≤nk\leq n in [5, 6, 7, 8, 9], considering general graphs when robots have prior knowledge of some parameters, while [10] studied the case without such knowledge in the local communication model, where robots at the same node can communicate. The problem has also been explored in other settings, such as dynamic graphs [11, 12], asynchronous models [5, 12], and the global communication model [13, 14]. Furthermore, dispersion has been studied on square grids [14, 15] and triangular grids [16].

Compared to Dispersion, Location-Aware Dispersion is more challenging, as some cases become unsolvable. For the solvable cases, the lower bounds are higher than the Dispersion lower bounds. Furthermore, parameter knowledge as well as initial configuration knowledge plays a significant role on what kind of solutions and guarantees can be achieved. Recently, Sudo et al. [9] established an important result in the synchronous setting by presenting two algorithms for general initial configurations: (i) a time-optimal O​(k)O(k) algorithm with memory O​(Δ+log⁡k)O(\Delta+\log k), and (ii) an O​(k​log2⁡k)O(k\log^{2}k)-time algorithm with memory O​(log⁡(k+Δ))O(\log(k+\Delta)). While the first result achieves optimal time, its memory requirement is prohibitively large, and while the second achieves near-optimal memory, it sacrifices time optimality. Kshemkalyani et al. [8] removed these limitations by presenting the first synchronous algorithm that simultaneously achieves both objectives: runs in optimal O​(k)O(k) rounds while requiring only O​(log⁡(k+Δ))O(\log(k+\Delta)) bits of memory per robot. This yields an O​(log2⁡k)O(\log^{2}k) factor reduction in time compared to best-known time-optimal result of [9], thereby closing the gap between time and memory optimality.

We study the Location-Aware Dispersion problem under rooted, dispersed, and general configurations, considering different assumptions on the robots knowledge of nn and kk. We further analyze Location-Aware Dispersion when the initial configuration is unknown.

In this section, we investigate fundamental limitations and performance guarantees of the Location-Aware Dispersion problem under deterministic robot models. We begin by establishing an impossibility result, showing that in certain settings the problem cannot be solved regardless of the amount of local memory available to the robots. We then derive a lower bound on the time and memory requirements that any deterministic solution must satisfy in the worst case. Finally, we identify and analyze several special cases, both in terms of graph structure and initial configurations, where these negative results can be circumvented, and efficient deterministic algorithms become possible. In particular, we present optimal or near-optimal solutions for trees, paths, and rings, as well as for rooted configurations in arbitrary graphs.

We show that under certain assumptions, the Location-Aware Dispersion problem admits no deterministic solution.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be an anonymous, port-labeled, undirected graph with nn nodes. For a single robot (k=1k=1), if nn is unknown, the Location-Aware Dispersion problem is unsolvable, even with unbounded local memory. But, if nn is known, the Location-Aware Dispersion problem is solvable in O~​(n5)\tilde{O}(n^{5}) time.

If the robot knows nn [4], it can compute and execute a Universal Exploration Sequence of length O~​(n5)\tilde{O}(n^{5}), which guarantees complete exploration of any anonymous, port-labeled graph with nn nodes, allowing it to solve Location-Aware Dispersion. If nn is unknown [2], a deterministic single robot in an anonymous graph cannot distinguish certain graph configurations and may be trapped in an infinite loop, repeatedly visiting the same nodes while unexplored nodes exist elsewhere. Consequently, it cannot guarantee complete exploration, even with unbounded local memory and the problem is unsolvable without prior knowledge of nn.
∎

We now establish our lower bound.

There is an initial configuration of k≤nk\leq n robots on a nn-node graph for which any deterministic algorithm for Location-Aware Dispersion requires
Ω​(min⁡{n2/k,m})\Omega(\min\{n^{2}/k,m\}) rounds and Ω​(n/k⋅log⁡k)\Omega(n/k\cdot\log k) bits per robot.

Consider a graph GG with nn nodes constructed as follows. Partition the nodes into n/kn/k groups (assume n/kn/k is an integer), each containing kk nodes. Denote the nodes in group ℓ\ell as vℓ​k+1,vℓ​k+2,…,vℓ​k+kv_{\ell k+1},v_{\ell k+2},\dots,v_{\ell k+k}, for 0≤ℓ≤n/k−10\leq\ell\leq n/k-1. Each group forms a complete graph on kk nodes. Within each group, remove the edges (ℓ​k+1,ℓ​k+k)(\ell k+1,\ell k+k) and (ℓ​k+2,ℓ​k+k−1)(\ell k+2,\ell k+k-1). Then, connect consecutive groups using bridge edges (ℓ​k+k,ℓ​k+k+1)(\ell k+k,\ell k+k+1) and (ℓ​k+k−1,ℓ​k+k+2)(\ell k+k-1,\ell k+k+2).

Assume there is a single red robot at v1v_{1}, and all nodes are blue except vnv_{n}, which is red. To achieve correct colorful dispersion, the robot must distinguish between different groups and track which nodes have already been visited.

Since there are n/kn/k groups, each group must be uniquely identifiable, which requires at least log⁡(n/k)\log(n/k) bits to encode the group identifiers. Within each group, the robot must deterministically explore the kk nodes to ensure correct placement and avoid revisiting nodes unnecessarily. At each step, the robot must select the correct port to reach unvisited nodes and eventually navigate the bridge edges to the next group. To encode its current position and make deterministic decisions within a group of kk nodes, the robot requires an additional log⁡k\log k bits of memory.

Combining these inter-group and intra-group requirements, each robot needs at least
Ω​((n/k)⋅log⁡k)\Omega\bigl((n/k)\cdot\log k\bigr) bits of memory to correctly maintain group information and ensure deterministic colorful dispersion on arbitrary graphs.
∎

We now discuss two special cases B1 and B2. B1 deals with special graphs: tree, path, and rings, whereas B2 deals with rooted initial configuration in arbitrary graphs with known k,nk,n and k=nk=n.

Tree, Path, Ring: Rooted, General or Dispersed Configuration, k≤nk\leq n (Algorithm 1): We run a DFS-based strategy. Each robot maintains two states: explore and settle. At each node vv, the minimum ID robot whose color matches the node color transitions to the settle state, while all other robots in the explore state exit the node through port-(pent+1)modδv(\textit{pent}+1)\bmod\delta_{v}, where pent is the port by which the robot entered vv and δv\delta_{v} is the degree of vv. This ensures systematic traversal without revisits, yielding a solution in O​(n)O(n) rounds. Initially, all robots start at one or more source nodes. In general, and in dispersed configurations, each group of robots, or a single robot, performs its DFS exploration independently. Robots that have settled on a node remain there, preventing conflicts, while other robots ignore occupied nodes and continue their exploration. This guarantees that at most one robot settles per node, achieving Location-Aware Dispersion. Each robot needs O​(log⁡(k+Δ))O(\log(k+\Delta)) bits to store its state, color, and port.

Tree, Path, Ring: Rooted, General or Dispersed Configuration, k≤nk\leq n (Algorithm 1): We run a DFS-based strategy. Each robot maintains two states: explore and settle. At each node vv, the minimum ID robot whose color matches the node color transitions to the settle state, while all other robots in the explore state exit the node through port-(pent+1)modδv(\textit{pent}+1)\bmod\delta_{v}, where pent is the port by which the robot entered vv and δv\delta_{v} is the degree of vv. This ensures systematic traversal without revisits, yielding a solution in O​(n)O(n) rounds. Initially, all robots start at one or more source nodes. In general, and in dispersed configurations, each group of robots, or a single robot, performs its DFS exploration independently. Robots that have settled on a node remain there, preventing conflicts, while other robots ignore occupied nodes and continue their exploration. This guarantees that at most one robot settles per node, achieving Location-Aware Dispersion. Each robot needs O​(log⁡(k+Δ))O(\log(k+\Delta)) bits to store its state, color, and port.

For any arbitrary initial configuration in a tree, path, and ring, Location-Aware Dispersion can be solved in O​(n)O(n) rounds using O​(log⁡(k+Δ))O(\log(k+\Delta)) bits per robot.

The proof directly follows from the standard DFS traversal. At each node vv, a robot rr settles if and only if 𝖼𝗈𝗅​(r)=𝖼𝗈𝗅​(v)\mathsf{col}(r)=\mathsf{col}(v) and rr has the minimum ID among the eligible robots. For a multi-source configuration, each source initiates its own DFS traversal. When a traversal encounters an already visited node, it continues its DFS without settling. If the node is unvisited, the robot with the minimum ID whose color matches the node settles there, and the remaining robots continue the traversal.

Consequently, the dispersion process completes in O​(m)O(m) rounds. For a tree or a path, m=n−1=O​(n)m=n-1=O(n), and for a ring, m=n=O​(n)m=n=O(n). Thus, in all these cases, the problem can be solved in O​(n)O(n) rounds. The memory used by the robots to store the variable is O​(log⁡(k+Δ))O(\log(k+\Delta)) bits.
∎

Arbitrary Graph, rooted Configuration, known n,kn,k, k=nk=n (Algorithm 2):  For k=nk=n robots starting from a rooted configuration, a DFS-based traversal ensures that each node receives exactly one robot. Each robot maintains a state (explore or settle) and a phase (forward or backtrack). In the forward phase, robots in the explore state move to unvisited nodes. At each node, the minimum-ID robot whose color matches the node color transitions to settle, while the others exit via (pent+1)modδv(\textit{pent}+1)\bmod\delta_{v}. When all children of a node are explored, robots enter the backtrack phase and return along the entry port, enabling systematic coverage of the graph. Settled robots store parent and child pointers to support forward and backtrack movement. This guarantees a solution to Location-Aware Dispersion in O​(m)O(m) using O​(log⁡(k+Δ))O(\log(k+\Delta)) bits per robot.

For any rooted initial configuration of k=nk=n robots in any arbitrary graph with k,nk,n known to robots, Location-Aware Dispersion can be solved in
O​(m)O(m) rounds using O​(log⁡k)O(\log k) bits per robot.

By the algorithm, the robots collectively perform a depth-first search (DFS) traversal starting from the source node SS. At each visited node vv, if the robot whose color matches vv is present, it settles permanently at vv, while the remaining robots continue the DFS traversal following the rules. Since DFS visits every node of GG, each node will eventually be reached. Moreover, as k=nk=n and for every color cic_{i} the number of robots with color cic_{i} equals the number of nodes of color cic_{i}. Hence, every node is eventually occupied by exactly one robot, and the Location-Aware Dispersion problem is solved.

The DFS explores each tree edge at most twice (once forward and once backtracking) and each non-tree edge at most four times. Thus, the total number of rounds is O​(m)O(m). Each robot only requires O​(log⁡k)O(\log k) bits to store the variables and its own ID.
∎

In this section, we consider the case where k<nk<n, with all kk robots initially located at a single source node SS. A traditional implementation of the DFS strategy from Section 2 (Cases B1 and B2) can cause robots to become trapped in cycles. The robots are constrained by limited memory and cannot store the complete path from the source to their intended destination nodes. During traversal, at each unvisited node, the unsettled robot with the smallest ID whose color matches the node settles there, while the remaining robots continue exploring. If no robot matches the node’s color, all proceed further. In graphs containing cycles of nodes whose colors do not correspond to any robot, the robots may circulate indefinitely, repeatedly revisiting the same nodes without reaching their target nodes. Consequently, a standard DFS strategy under such memory constraints does not guarantee dispersion and may result in deadlocks. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel DFS-based procedure organized into three systematic phases, ensuring that each robot eventually reaches a node of matching color and terminates solving Location-Aware Dispersion.

We assume k=⌈n/c⌉k=\lceil n/c\rceil with c≤nc\leq n a constant. Since, in the rooted setting, all robots are collocated at a single source node, which allows them to identify the total number of robots kk. Thus, whether kk is initially known or unknown does not affect the model in the rooted configuration.

The graph nodes are organized into “groups” of designated sizes, and one robot in each group is designated as the “guard” (referred to as leader or oscillating in algorithm) of that group. The group sizes are not fixed, but are bounded above and below, and are determined based on kk and nn. Once the DFS traversal is completed, the guard robot at the source node SS detects its completion. The algorithm also identifies a set of edges connecting the groups called “inter-group edges”. Each group records its parent port (the port leading to its parent group) and child ports (the ports leading to its child groups) w.r.t. these edges. These inter-group edges are guaranteed to be cycle-free. Treating each group as a “supernode”, the groups and inter-group edges collectively form an oriented rooted tree 𝒯{\cal T}, rooted at the supernode containing SS (“root supernode”). The DFS traversal completes once the root supernode contains at least two robots.

The group sizes are not fixed, but are bounded above and below, and are determined based on kk and nn. Once the DFS traversal is completed, the guard robot at the source node SS detects its completion. The algorithm also identifies a set of edges connecting the groups called “inter-group edges”. Each group records its parent port (the port leading to its parent group) and child ports (the ports leading to its child groups) w.r.t. these edges. These inter-group edges are guaranteed to be cycle-free. Treating each group as a “supernode”, the groups and inter-group edges collectively form an oriented rooted tree 𝒯{\cal T}, rooted at the supernode containing SS (“root supernode”). The DFS traversal completes once the root supernode contains at least two robots.

After Phase 1, the goal is to aggregate robots at SS to get the complete connectivity of each node of the graph. The guard robot at root supernode initiates a DFS on 𝒯{\cal T}. Along this traversal, it brings other robots with it, and eventually all robots return to SS. Each robot stores a portion of the graph structure, and collectively they have the complete connectivity information of nodes in the graph at the source SS.

The final task is dispersion. Since robots have connectivity information of each node, that locally determine their destination supernodes (and the specific nodes within them). Each robot must eventually travel from SS to its assigned supernode. However, due to memory constraints, we cannot provide each robot with the full path information. To address this, we propose a two-phase mechanism: (i) in the first phase, the path from each target supernode to the root supernode SS is established by keeping one robot per supernode; (ii) in the second phase, the required number of robots move toward their designated supernodes along these paths, before finally reaching their exact destination nodes.

Several key questions arise in each phase, each presenting challenges. We proceed to address them one by one:

How does the DFS traversal operate, with groups being formed during the process? (refer to Fig. 1)

How does the DFS traversal operate, with groups being formed during the process? (refer to Fig. 1)

In Location-Aware Dispersion, the strategy follows DFS, with the additional requirement of forming groups of nodes of specified sizes (see Q2) during the traversal. Groups are formed incrementally as the DFS progresses. In the forward phase, robots move collectively along unexplored edges, assigning the lowest-ID robot to settle within each newly created group (see Q3), and includes the unvisited nodes in the group as the traversal proceeds (see Q2). As exploration proceeds, the leader records parent–child relationships and expands the group until its size reaches valid threshold (see Q3). Once a group is formed, the robot corresponding to that group remains in the group, while remaining robots continue traversal to create subsequent groups.

During the traversal, if a robot encounters a visited node i.e., belongs to an existing group, it either backtracks along explored edges to continue the DFS, or the existing group and current group may dynamically shrink or expand according to the exploration process (see Q5). Whenever a group reaches the required size, a new group is initiated (see Q4). The traversal completes once all nodes have been explored and at least one robot has returned to the source node (see Q7).

What is the group structure?

Each group consists of two types of nodes: required and helper: required nodes form the core of the group, as they must ultimately be occupied by robots of matching color in the final dispersion, and helper nodes are additional nodes included only to preserve the connectivity of the group; they typically lie along simple paths connecting pairs of required nodes. Each group designates a required node as its source node. The subgraph induced by a group is always connected, and can be represented as a tree rooted at the group’s source node. The guard robot associated with a group maintains the list of required and helper nodes. A crucial constraint is that each required node belongs uniquely to exactly one group, whereas helper nodes serve as required nodes for some other group, ensuring non-overlapping coverage of required nodes across groups. Additionally, each group maintains information about its inter-group edges, which define the parent–child relationships among groups (see Q6). During Phases 2 and 3, each group can be abstracted as a single supernode111With slight abuse of terminology, we use the terms supernode and group interchangeably, as they denote the same object with different interpretations. The terminology inter-group edges remains unchanged.. Consequently, the structure formed by treating groups (or supernodes) as vertices and inter-group edges as connections between them constitutes an oriented rooted tree 𝒯{\cal T}.

What is the size of a group?

Formally, let c=Θ​(n/k)c=\Theta(n/k), and assume k=⌈n/c⌉k=\lceil n/c\rceil robots with limited memory are initially placed at the source SS. If at most ⌈n/c⌉\lceil n/c\rceil distinct groups are formed, each of size between 2​c2c and 4​c4c required nodes, and exactly one robot is assigned as the guard of each group, then complete exploration of the graph is guaranteed: every node of GG belongs to exactly one group as a required node, and the collective memory of the robots suffices to store connectivity information about all nn nodes.

If group sizes are restricted to [c,2​c][c,2c], at most kk distinct groups can form; however, no robot may return to the source, preventing DFS completion (see Q8). To avoid this, we consider groups of size between 2​c2c and 4​c4c. A group becomes valid upon reaching 2​c2c required nodes, ensuring enough robots to guard all nodes and maintain exploration invariants, while exceeding 4​c4c triggers a split or restructuring. Since each group has between 2​c2c and 4​c4c required nodes, at most 2​c−12c-1 helper nodes suffice to maintain its tree structure. Thus, each group contains at most 6​c6c nodes in total. This guarantees that traversal within a group by its guard robot takes only O​(c)O(c) rounds (see Q4).

How does a robot determine, upon reaching a node, whether the node has already been explored? (refer to Fig. 1(d))

Each group is a rooted tree and can have at most 6​c6c nodes (at most 4​c4c required and at most 2​c−12c-1 helper nodes). The guard robot oscillates between the nodes within its group, and thus it requires at most 12​c12c rounds to visit every node in that group at least once. Consequently, any robot rr that is not a guard robot at a node vv waits for 12​c12c rounds. After 12​c12c rounds, if the robot rr encounters the guard robot corresponding to the node vv (required node for the guard robot) or vv is required node of rr, it learns that vv has already been visited; otherwise, rr determines that it is visiting vv for the first time.

How does the group size shrink or expand during the traversal? (refer to Fig. 1(d) ⟶\longrightarrow Fig. 1(e))

A guard robot rr expands its group during DFS traversal until it contains 4​c4c required nodes. Except for a special case, once the group size reaches at least 2​c2c and rr encounters an already visited node, it stops expanding, as the group is considered sufficient. Robot rr shrinks its group when, during the backtrack phase (of DFS), it meets another guard robot r′r^{\prime} at a required node vv of its group and its group size is less than 2​c2c. If all children of vv have been explored, robot rr reduces its group size and transfers information about the required nodes in the subtree rooted at vv. Based on its own group size, robot r′r^{\prime} stores information about nodes farther from vv.

How are inter-group edges identified? (refer to Fig. 1(b) →\rightarrow Fig. 1(c))

An inter-group edge is defined as an edge (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E where two required nodes uu and vv are from two different groups. These edges are identified naturally during DFS: when robots attempt to move along an edge into a node that is already claimed by another group by a robot that recently became a guard robot of that group (as in Q1), they mark that edge as an inter-group edge. Each group records the port numbers of such edges as part of its local data. Collectively, these inter-group edges form the parent-child relationships between groups.

How do robots detect the end of DFS? (refer to Fig. 1(g) →\rightarrow Fig. 1(h))

The completion of the traversal is detected at the source group (the group that contains the source node). The guard robot at the source maintains a counter that records the number of completed explorations through each incident port, which is incremented by 1 when an incident port is explored. Since each port is explored and returned through exactly twice (forward and backward), the guard concludes that the DFS traversal is complete once its counter reaches δS\delta_{S}, where δS\delta_{S} is the degree of the source node. At this point, all groups have been created, all inter-group edges identified, and all nodes of the graph visited, ensuring that the traversal is complete.

How do robots maintain synchrony during DFS traversal?

During DFS traversal, robots are divided into three types: (i) those that continue moving along the DFS path, (ii) the guard robot, which oscillates within its group, and (iii) the recent guard robot, which oscillates within its group and is responsible for forming a new group. The recent guard robot also moves with the DFS-traversing robots, as it expands its group by visiting unexplored nodes (maintaining the oscillation as well). Time is divided into intermediate rounds and movement rounds to maintain synchrony. In an intermediate round, robots wait at their current node to verify whether it has been visited (see Q4). During this period, the guard robot (both previous and recent ones) oscillates; if it encounters another robot, it shares information and either returns to its group’s source node or waits at the current node, depending on the type of communication. Other robots continue to wait and perform computations if they encounter an oscillating guard robot. In the movement round, robots proceed with the DFS traversal to the next node. This structured division ensures that all robots remain synchronized during each node visit.

Note that after Phase 1, the set of supernodes together with the inter-group edges forms an oriented rooted tree 𝒯{\cal T}, rooted at the supernode containing the source node SS. Since robots outside the source supernode do not know when Phase 1 terminates, Phase 2 proceeds differently. This phase employs a classical DFS traversal on 𝒯{\cal T}, with two main challenges:

The guard robot rr at SS initiates the traversal. During the forward phase, rr explores new supernodes, guided by the guard robots at those supernodes. When the DFS backtracks from a supernode WW, the guard robot at WW joins the traversal and moves along the backtracking path toward its parent. By the time the traversal completes the subtree rooted at WW, all robots within that subtree have already been collected and are en route to SS.

The guard robot rr at SS initiates the traversal. During the forward phase, rr explores new supernodes, guided by the guard robots at those supernodes. When the DFS backtracks from a supernode WW, the guard robot at WW joins the traversal and moves along the backtracking path toward its parent. By the time the traversal completes the subtree rooted at WW, all robots within that subtree have already been collected and are en route to SS.

Synchronization is maintained in the same manner as in Phase 1. Specifically, when rr reaches a supernode, it spends sufficient time there to ensure that it encounters the guard robot located at that supernode, thereby aligning the traversal across the tree.

Acyclicity. A vertex is added to UrU_{r} exactly once: either upon its first visit during the forward traversal (as a required node) or during the backtrack phase when robot rr expands its group and incorporates vertices from another group as helper or required nodes. During the execution, robot rr may expand or shrink its group.

During the forward traversal, if robot rr encounters a vertex u∈Uru\in U_{r} that has already been visited (i.e., u∈Qru\in Q_{r} or u∈Hru\in H_{r}), the active robot detects this condition and, after the prescribed waiting time, backtracks without adding any edge. Hence, no edge is added between two previously visited vertices in the forward phase.

During the backtracking phase, robot rr may expand its group upon reaching a vertex v∈Qr′v\in Q_{r^{\prime}} for some robot r′r^{\prime}. The expansion follows a simple path, and for each newly added vertex, exactly one edge, connecting it to its predecessor on the path is added to ErE_{r}. Suppose, for contradiction, that this expansion creates a cycle. Then some newly added vertex v′v^{\prime} must be connected to a vertex u∈Uru\in U_{r} that was already present before the expansion. This would imply that the robot rr traversed the edge from v′v^{\prime} to uu, establishing a parent-child relationship with v′v^{\prime} as the parent. However, during the backtracking phase, traversal is allowed only from a child to its parent; thus, the robot rr would have backtracked from uu to v′v^{\prime}, a contradiction. Therefore, no cycle is formed during expansion.

Finally, when the robot rr shrinks its group, vertices and their incident edges are removed. Since edge deletions cannot create cycles, acyclicity is preserved.

Thus, in all cases, the subgraph (Ur,Er)(U_{r},E_{r}) maintained by robot rr is acyclic.

Suppose, for contradiction, that there exists a vertex w∉Frw\notin F_{r} lying on the path between uu and vv. Finally, when robot rr shrinks its group, connectivity is preserved, as after the shrinking operation, either the vertex vv continues to belong to FrF_{r}, or it is removed along with its dependent subtree, ensuring that the remaining vertices in FrF_{r} remain connected.

Moreover, since the exploration maintains acyclicity, this path is unique. Therefore, the subgraph induced by FrF_{r} is connected.

In this section, we study the Location-Aware Dispersion problem under a rooted configuration, where all kk robots are initially colocated at a single source node SS. The total number of nodes nn in the graph is unknown. As in the rooted setting, all robots are initially colocated at a single node, enabling each of them to determine the total number of robots kk. Thus, whether kk is initially known or unknown does not affect the model in the rooted configuration.

The core idea is to enable robots to explore an arbitrary graph without prior knowledge of nn by iterative guessing with DFS-based exploration (as in Section 3). Since the known-nn strategy of Section 3 relies on bounding DFS by nn, robots begin with the assumption n=kn=k and initiate a DFS, where each node is assigned to at most one robot and groups are coordinated by the oscillating robot at each group. If the traversal completes and all robots are placed without leaving nodes unexplored, the guess is correct and dispersion succeeds. Otherwise, the inability to settle all robots (or the discovery of unexplored nodes) reveals that the guess was too small. In this case, all robots backtrack and regroup at SS, the assumed value of nn is doubled, and a new DFS attempt is initiated. By progressively doubling the guess, the robots eventually reach an interval [2i​k,2i+1​k][2^{i}k,2^{i+1}k] that contains the true nn, ensuring that dispersion is completed in that iteration. This strategy guarantees correctness regardless of the initial underestimate of nn, while incurring only a logarithmic overhead of O​(log⁡(n/k))O(\log(n/k)) in number of DFS trials compared to the known-nn setting. Once the graph exploration phase is completed, the gathering and dispersion steps from Section 3 are applied, thereby completing Location-Aware Dispersion.

Location-Aware Dispersion can be solved deterministically in rooted initial configuration with k>1k>1 robots having no prior knowledge of nn in O​(log⁡(n/k)⋅n/k⋅m)O(\log(n/k)\cdot n/k\cdot m) rounds using O​(n/k⋅log⁡(k+Δ))O(n/k\cdot\log(k+\Delta)) bits per robot.

The algorithm follows an iterative guessing strategy combined with DFS-based exploration.

Initially, the robots assume that n=kn=k and perform a bounded DFS starting from the source node SS. During this traversal, one robot is assigned to each group, ensuring that every group contains at least 2​c2c and at most 4​c4c nodes. If the traversal completes successfully, that is, if c​o​u​n​t=δS−1count=\delta_{S}-1 and some robots return to the source node SS, then dispersion is achieved by Lemma 2.

Otherwise, suppose that during the exploration only one active robot remains and it detects the existence of unexplored nodes. This implies that the traversal is incomplete. In this situation, the remaining active robot becomes a leader, and no active robot returns to SS, which contradicts Lemma 2. Hence, the current estimate underestimates the actual value of nn. In this case, all robots return to the source node SS by backtracking along the DFS traversal, double the guessed value of nn, and repeat the DFS process.

Since the guessed value of nn doubles in each iteration, after O​(log⁡(n/k))O(\log(n/k)) iterations, the estimate becomes sufficiently accurate, and the DFS completes successfully. Each DFS attempt requires O​(n/k⋅m)O(n/k\cdot m) rounds, as established in the known-nn case (Theorem 4). Therefore, the total round complexity of the algorithm is O​(log⁡(n/k)⋅n/k⋅m)O(\log(n/k)\cdot n/k\cdot m).

The memory requirement per robot remains the same as in the known-nn setting, since robots store only local DFS state and coordination information. Consequently, each robot uses O​(n/k⋅log⁡(k+Δ))O(n/k\cdot\log(k+\Delta)) bits of memory.

Hence, the dispersion problem in a rooted configuration with unknown nn can be solved deterministically within the stated time and memory bounds.

We study Location-Aware Dispersion for general initial configurations, that is, there exists a source node ss in the graph GG that initially hosts at least two robots. In any general initial configuration, a node hosting exactly one robot is called a s​i​n​g​l​esingle source, while a node containing at least two robots is a m​u​l​t​imulti source. Our approach builds on the multi-source DFS framework of Kshemkalyani and Sharma [7], which is applied to classical dispersion and adapted to preserve the group structure required for Location-Aware Dispersion.

High level idea: A robot located at a s​i​n​g​l​esingle source remains at its current node, since a single robot without node memory cannot explore the graph, as discussed in Section 2. In contrast, robots at a m​u​l​t​imulti-source initiate a DFS traversal, forming bounded-size groups coordinated by a designated oscillating robot (as in Section 2). When two DFS traversals meet at a node or encounter a s​i​n​g​l​esingle-source robot, a subsumption step is executed. The traversal with more settled robots survives, while the smaller traversal is collapsed and its robots are reassigned to the surviving DFS; ties are broken by the minimum treelabel. Multiple simultaneous collisions are resolved via pairwise subsumptions. Over time, the number of concurrent DFS traversals decreases, ensuring that eventually a single traversal remains.

When k=nk=n and both kk and nn are known, each source starts a DFS forming groups of size [2​c,4​c][2c,4c], and subsumption ensures that the dominant traversal continues exploration.

Algorithm: Each robot initializes a treelabel as the minimum-ID robot at its source and a gr_num counter recording the number of settled robots. The s​i​n​g​l​esingle-source robot changes its state to w​a​i​twait and remains at its current node until it is discovered and merged into a passing DFS traversal. Each m​u​l​t​imulti-source initiates a bounded DFS traversal, where DFS heads traverse the graph, forming groups of size [2​c,4​c][2c,4c]. When a DFS head reaches a node, robots wait a fixed interval to detect collisions with other DFS traversals. Subsumption rules are applied deterministically, where the traversal is guided by the robots responsible for the groups, and the traversal with more settled robots survives, and the others are merged. Each robot in a subsumed traversal is reassigned to the surviving DFS, which may revisit each node of the collapsed traversal at most once. When a surviving DFS encounters a s​i​n​g​l​esingle-source robot, that robot is immediately merged into the traversal and becomes part of its settled group.

Consider a connected graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) with |V|=n|V|=n and k=n>1k=n>1 robots in a general initial configuration, where each robot knows nn and kk. Each robot initializes a treelabel and a gr_num counter equal to the number of settled robots at its source.

Each multi-source robot initiates a bounded DFS traversal, forming groups of size [2​c,4​c][2c,4c]. When two DFS traversals collide, a deterministic subsumption rule is applied: the traversal with more settled robots survives, and the other is merged. Since group sizes strictly increase, the number of active traversals decreases monotonically, ensuring termination. Single-source robots remain in the w​a​i​twait state until discovered and are then merged into a passing DFS.

Each subsumed traversal may cause nodes to be revisited, but each node is revisited at most once. Thus, each DFS explores O​(m)O(m) edges, and since at most O​(n/k)O(n/k) DFS traversals survive sequentially, the total running time is O​(n/k⋅m)O(n/k\cdot m) rounds.

Each robot stores a treelabel, a group counter, and DFS state, requiring O​(n/k⋅log⁡k)O(n/k\cdot\log k) bits of memory.

Hence, Location-Aware Dispersion is solved deterministically in general initial configurations within the stated time and memory bounds.
∎

We consider the setting where robots may or may not know nn and kk.

Algorithm: Each source SpS_{p} initiates a DFS with an initial guess n=kpn=k_{p}, forming bounded-size groups coordinated by oscillating robots. The main challenge is that independent DFSs may never meet at arbitrary nodes due to differences in group sizes and unsynchronized oscillations between groups of different DFSs. Consequently, merging cannot rely on incidental encounters during exploration.

To guarantee convergence, each source retains a p​a​s​s​i​v​epassive robot. Since each DFS traversal is guaranteed to eventually visit every node, any traversal reaching a source will encounter its p​a​s​s​i​v​epassive robot and merge with the traversal originating there. However, an additional challenge arises when sources contain exactly two robots.

Let us consider the source where exactly two robots are present at a source ss. To guarantee convergence, one robot remains at ss in a p​a​s​s​i​v​epassive state while the other initiates exploration. However, a single robot cannot explore an anonymous graph, as discussed earlier in Section 1.

This leads us to two possible cases, depending on the initial configuration of sources.

Case 1: If there exists at least one source initially hosting more than two robots: Suppose there exists a source SS that initially contains at least three robots. In this setting, the DFS initiated at SS can proceed normally, leaving one p​a​s​s​i​v​epassive robot at the source. Whenever this DFS encounters another traversal or a s​i​n​g​l​esingle-source robot, merging occurs according to the standard subsumption rule: the traversal with more settled robots continues, and the smaller traversal is absorbed. As a result, all robots eventually gather at the dominant traversal’s source and continue exploration as a single unified DFS.

If some other source initially contains exactly two robots, those two robots start a DFS without leaving behind a p​a​s​s​i​v​epassive robot, since a single robot cannot explore. Their traversal will eventually reach the source SS, where the p​a​s​s​i​v​epassive robot remains, and will merge into the DFS originating from SS.

Therefore, the existence of even one source with at least three robots guarantees global convergence: all DFS processes eventually merge into one, which explores the entire graph and subsequently performs dispersion.

This scenario requires only O​(n/k⋅log⁡(k+Δ))O(n/k\cdot\log(k+\Delta)) bits of memory per robot, matching the memory bound of the general algorithm.

Case 2: If there does not exist at least one source initially hosting more than two robots: Consider a source SS that initially contains exactly two robots. Since a single robot cannot explore, both robots initiate independent bounded DFS traversals, leaving no p​a​s​s​i​v​epassive robot at the source. There are two possible cases:

If either of the two robots of source SS encounters another DFS traversal or a s​i​n​g​l​esingle-source robot, merging occurs according to the standard subsumption rule: the traversal containing more settled robots continues, while the smaller traversal is absorbed. Once merging results in a source with more than two robots, the process switches to Case 1: one robot becomes p​a​s​s​i​v​epassive at the source, and the remaining robots initiate a new DFS.

If either of the two robots of source SS encounters another DFS traversal or a s​i​n​g​l​esingle-source robot, merging occurs according to the standard subsumption rule: the traversal containing more settled robots continues, while the smaller traversal is absorbed. Once merging results in a source with more than two robots, the process switches to Case 1: one robot becomes p​a​s​s​i​v​epassive at the source, and the remaining robots initiate a new DFS.

If no encounters take place during the exploration, this situation indicates that every source (if it exists) initially contained exactly two robots and that the DFS traversals originating from different sources remained completely disjoint throughout their execution. Since none of the traversals interacted or merged with any other traversal or s​i​n​g​l​esingle-source robot, each pair of robots independently completes its bounded exploration and acquires full knowledge of the graph GG. The two robots at the source SS then disperse to distinct nearest nodes based on a matching between node colors and robot colors. If a node is already occupied by another robot, a robot uses its stored knowledge to move to the next nearest available node. In the event that two or more robots reach the same node simultaneously, tie-breaking is performed using their unique IDs.

This process ensures successful dispersion, but it requires each robot to store complete graph knowledge, resulting in a memory requirement of O​(n​log⁡(k+Δ))O(n\log(k+\Delta)) bits per robot.

Location-Aware Dispersion can be solved deterministically in general initial configuration in O​(log⁡(n/k)⋅n/k⋅m)O(\log(n/k)\cdot n/k\cdot m) rounds. The algorithm requires (i) O​(n/k⋅log⁡(k+Δ))O(n/k\cdot\log(k+\Delta)) bits of memory per robot if some source initially hosts at least three robots, and (ii) O​(n⋅log⁡(k+Δ))O(n\cdot\log(k+\Delta)) bits of memory per robot otherwise.

We prove the theorem by contradiction. Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that the algorithm does not solve the Location-Aware Dispersion problem under the stated conditions. Then at least one of the following must hold:

(i) the algorithm does not terminate, or
(ii) it terminates but fails to achieve correct dispersion.

Assume that the algorithm does not terminate. Then infinitely many DFS phases are executed without achieving convergence.

Consider any DFS phase. Either at least two DFS traversals intersect, or they do not. If two DFS traversals intersect, then by the subsumption rule, exactly one traversal survives, and the other is absorbed. Hence, the total number of active DFS traversals strictly decreases. Since the number of sources is finite, this process cannot continue indefinitely. Therefore, infinitely many phases without termination is impossible in this case.

Otherwise, suppose that no DFS traversals intersect in a given phase. Then each traversal completes its bounded exploration and returns to its source. By the algorithm, the exploration capacity is increased exponentially in the next phase. Since the graph GG is finite, after finitely many phases, the exploration range of at least one traversal becomes large enough to intersect another traversal or reach a source containing a passive robot. This again forces subsumption and reduces the number of DFS traversals.

Thus, in every phase, either the number of traversals strictly decreases or the exploration capacity increases. Both quantities are bounded, implying that the algorithm must terminate. This contradicts the assumption of non-termination.

Assume now that the algorithm terminates but does not achieve dispersion. If the execution reaches a configuration with exactly one active DFS traversal, then the situation reduces to the rooted case. By correctness of the rooted algorithm (by Lemma 4), dispersion is achieved, contradicting the assumption.

Otherwise, suppose the algorithm terminates with multiple DFS traversals that never merged. This can occur only if every source initially contains exactly two robots and no traversal ever intersects another. In this case, each DFS eventually completes its exploration and acquires complete knowledge of the graph. Using this information, each pair of robots disperses to distinct nodes via deterministic tie-breaking. Hence, dispersion is still achieved, contradicting the assumption.

Since both non-termination and incorrect termination lead to contradictions, the algorithm must terminate and correctly solve the Location-Aware Dispersion problem.

Each DFS phase requires O​(n/k⋅m)O(n/k\cdot m) rounds, and the exploration capacity doubles in each phase, yielding O​(log⁡(n/k))O(\log(n/k)) phases. Thus, the total round complexity is O​(log⁡(n/k)⋅n/k⋅m)O(\log(n/k)\cdot n/k\cdot m). The memory bounds follow directly from whether robots store partial or complete graph information, as stated in the theorem. Hence, the theorem holds.
∎

In this subsection, we study the Location-Aware Dispersion problem under dispersed initial configurations, where each node of the graph initially hosts at most one robot. Thus, k=nk=n robots are placed on nn distinct nodes of an arbitrary graph GG, and both kk and nn are known to all robots.

Our approach builds upon the “meeting protocol for two adjacent agents” in [3], which guarantees that two adjacent agents meet within O​(log⁡L)O(\log L) rounds, where LL is the ID of highest ID robot. Over time, the initially dispersed configuration evolves into a general configuration, in which at least one node hosts two or more robots.

Meeting protocol for two adjacent agents: Consider two robots rur_{u} and rvr_{v} initially located at adjacent nodes uu and vv of the graph, where uu is connected to vv via an outgoing port pup_{u} at uu. The goal is for robot rur_{u} to meet its neighbour rvr_{v} through port pup_{u}. Each robot first pads its ID to a log⁡L\log L-bit binary string and then appends its bitwise complement to the left, thereby forming a new ID of length 2​log⁡L2\log L bits, where log⁡L\log L is the length of the largest ID robot. The protocol proceeds bit by bit, from the least significant bit (LSB) to the most significant bit (MSB). For each bit position ii, if the ii-th bit of rur_{u}’s new ID is 11, the robot moves from node uu to node vv in the first round of the pair and returns to uu in the second; if the bit is 0, the robot remains at uu for both rounds. Since all robots have distinct IDs, there exists at least one bit position at which one robot’s new ID has a 11 while the other has a 0. In that round, one robot moves while the other remains still, ensuring that the two robots meet.

Thus, the protocol completes in 4​log⁡L4\log L rounds, with two rounds devoted to each bit position. The protocol is entirely local and requires no knowledge of the state or behaviour of rvr_{v}. A robot may invoke this procedure using any specific port it intends to traverse.

Note that in [3], the robots are assumed to have prior knowledge of log⁡L\log L. In our setting, the robots know the value of nn, and each robot with an ID in [1,kO​(1)][1,k^{O(1)}] and therefore is assumed to know its value.

Algorithm: Initially, all robots are in a dispersed configuration, and each robot knows the value of nn. Every robot rr positioned at a node uu initiates the Meeting Protocol for Two Adjacent Agents by attempting to visit its neighbor vv through port 0. During the execution of this protocol, if robot rr meets another robot r′r^{\prime} at node vv, it forms a group with r′r^{\prime} and thereafter follows r′r^{\prime}, while r′r^{\prime} continues executing the algorithm. By repeatedly applying this protocol across all adjacent pairs, robots located on neighboring nodes are guaranteed to meet. After at most 4​log⁡k4\log k rounds, the initially dispersed configuration transforms into a general configuration in which at least one node hosts two or more robots.

Once such a general configuration is obtained, we apply the algorithm developed for the general initial setting (Section 5), which guarantees deterministic Location-Aware Dispersion for arbitrary placements with k=nk=n.

Location-Aware Dispersion can be solved deterministically in dispersed initial configuration with k=nk=n robots having prior knowledge of n,kn,k in O​(log⁡(k)+n/k⋅m)O(\log(k)+n/k\cdot m) rounds using O​(n/k⋅log⁡k)O(n/k\cdot\log k) bits per robot.

We prove correctness, termination, and complexity of the algorithm.

Initially, the robots are in a dispersed configuration, with exactly one robot per node and with full knowledge of nn and k=nk=n. Each robot independently initiates the Meeting Protocol for Two Adjacent Agents with one of its neighbors. By the properties of the protocol, any two robots located at adjacent nodes are guaranteed to meet within O​(log⁡L)O(\log L) rounds.

Since the graph GG is connected, repeated executions of the meeting protocol ensure that at least one pair of adjacent robots meets, forming a group of size at least two. Once such a meeting occurs, the configuration is no longer dispersed and becomes a general configuration, in which at least one node hosts multiple robots.

After reaching a general configuration, the robots execute the deterministic algorithm for the general initial setting described in Section 5. By Theorem 7, this algorithm correctly solves the Location-Aware Dispersion problem for arbitrary initial placements with known nn, ensuring that all robots are placed on distinct nodes and that each node hosts at most one robot. Hence, correctness follows.

The meeting phase requires at most O​(log⁡L)O(\log L) rounds to transform the dispersed configuration into a general configuration. Once this occurs, the algorithm for the general setting requires O​(log⁡(n/k)⋅n/k⋅m)O(\log(n/k)\cdot n/k\cdot m) rounds. Since k=nk=n in the dispersed setting, the total round complexity is O​(log⁡(L)+log⁡(n/k)⋅n/k⋅m)O(\log(L)+\log(n/k)\cdot n/k\cdot m). Hence, the time and memory complexity follow from Theorem 7.
∎

We study the Location-Aware Dispersion problem under dispersed initial configurations for k<nk<n robots, where each node of the graph initially hosts at most one robot. Thus, kk robots occupy kk distinct nodes of an arbitrary graph GG, and both kk and nn are known to all robots.

The high-level idea is to transform the dispersed configuration into a general configuration, i.e., a configuration in which at least one node hosts two or more robots. Once such a source exists, the Location-Aware Dispersion problem becomes solvable using the techniques developed for general configurations.

This transformation is closely related to the classical deterministic gathering problem. In particular, the work [4] addresses the setting in which kk robots are placed on the nodes of an nn-node graph, with the objective of having all kk robots meet at a single node and terminate. They present deterministic algorithms that achieve gathering with detection on arbitrary graphs.

The authors first present a universal exploration sequence (UXS)-based gathering algorithm that requires O~​(n5)\tilde{O}(n^{5}) rounds. They then focus on undispersed configurations (where some nodes initially host multiple robots), and propose a more efficient two-phase algorithm. In the first phase, a group of robots collaboratively constructs a map of the graph in O​(n3)O(n^{3}) rounds, while in the second phase, this map is used to route all robots to a designated gathering node.

They then address the dispersed configuration by first attempting to convert it into an undispersed configuration. The resulting time complexity depends on the minimum distance between any two robots. If the closest pair of robots is at distance ii, the robots meet and form an undispersed configuration in O​(ni​log⁡n)O(n^{i}\log n) rounds. Subsequently, all robots gather at a designated node in O~​(n5)\tilde{O}(n^{5}) rounds.

Hence, the following complexity trade-offs hold for gathering all robots at a single node from a dispersed configuration:

The gathering completes in O​(n3)O(n^{3}) rounds if the initial configuration is undispersed, or if it is dispersed with at least two robots located at distance 22 from each other.

The gathering completes in O​(ni​log⁡n)O(n^{i}\log n) rounds if the initial configuration is dispersed with at least two robots located at distance ii, for i∈{3,4,5}i\in\{3,4,5\}.

Otherwise, the gathering requires O~​(n5)\tilde{O}(n^{5}) rounds.

Consequently, the following bounds hold as a function of the number of robots kk, for arbitrary initial configurations:

If k≥⌊n/2⌋+1k\geq\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1, the gathering completes in O​(n3)O(n^{3}) rounds.

If k≥⌊n/3⌋+1k\geq\lfloor n/3\rfloor+1, the gathering completes in O​(n4​log⁡n)O(n^{4}\log n) rounds.

Otherwise, the gathering requires O~​(n5)\tilde{O}(n^{5}) rounds.

Importantly, the algorithm assumes knowledge of the graph size nn but does not require knowledge of the number of robots kk.

Algorithm: Our approach builds upon the results of [4]. Since the robots know kk or nn, they can gather at a single node by directly applying the deterministic gathering routines from that work. In particular, if the closest pair of robots is at distance i∈{1,2,3,4,5}i\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}, then the gathering completes in O​(ni​log⁡n)O(n^{i}\log n) rounds. Once such a general configuration is obtained, we invoke the algorithm designed for the general initial setting (Section 5).

If no such pair of robots exists, the gathering procedure brings all robots to a single node in O~​(n5)\tilde{O}(n^{5}) rounds. After this rooted configuration is formed, we apply the algorithm developed for the rooted initial setting (Section 3).

The Location-Aware Dispersion problem can be solved deterministically in a dispersed initial configuration with k<nk<n robots and prior knowledge of nn, using O​(M∗+n/k⋅log⁡(k+Δ))O(M^{*}+n/k\cdot\log(k+\Delta)) bits of memory per robot, where M∗M^{*} denotes the memory required to implement a Universal Exploration Sequence (UXS). The time complexity is: (i) O​(n3+n/k⋅m)O(n^{3}+n/k\cdot m) rounds if i=1,2i=1,2, where ii is the distance between the closest pair of robots; (ii) O​(ni​log⁡n+n/k⋅m)O(n^{i}\log n+n/k\cdot m) rounds if i∈{3,4,5}i\in\{3,4,5\}; (iii) O~​(n5)\tilde{O}(n^{5}) rounds otherwise.

Initially, the robots are in a dispersed configuration with k<nk<n robots placed on distinct nodes of a connected graph GG, and all robots know nn and kk. The goal is to transform this dispersed configuration into a configuration for which the Location-Aware Dispersion problem is already solvable.

The algorithm first applies a deterministic gathering procedure from [4]. This procedure guarantees that all robots gather at a single node or that at least one node hosts multiple robots, depending on the distance between the closest pair of robots. In either case, the resulting configuration is no longer dispersed.

If the gathering procedure results in a general configuration, that is, a configuration in which at least one node hosts two or more robots, we invoke the algorithm for general initial configurations (Section 5). By Theorem 7, this algorithm correctly solves the Location-Aware Dispersion problem.

If the gathering procedure results in a rooted configuration, in which all robots gather at a single node, we apply the algorithm for rooted initial configurations (Section 3). By the correctness of that algorithm, dispersion is achieved deterministically.

Thus, in all cases, the algorithm produces a correct colorful dispersion.

From [4], if the closest pair of robots is at distance i∈{2,3,4,5}i\in\{2,3,4,5\}, the gathering phase completes in O​(ni​log⁡n)O(n^{i}\log n) rounds. If no such pair exists, the gathering phase completes in O~​(n5)\tilde{O}(n^{5}) rounds. Once the gathering phase terminates, the resulting configuration is either
rooted or general. In both cases, the subsequent execution preserves the asymptotic bounds, and thus the claimed time and memory complexities follow.
∎

For known nn, if the configuration is rooted and kk is known, the robots can immediately detect this and solve the problem using the algorithm of Section 3.
For all other situations, the robots first gather at a single node, thereby creating a rooted configuration, using the result of Molla et al. [4], deterministic gathering with detection is possible on arbitrary graphs using only the knowledge of nn, via universal exploration sequences.
When the initial configuration is already rooted but kk is unknown, the robots explore the graph to enable correct identification. Once a rooted configuration is formed and nn is known, the robots apply the rooted algorithm (Section 3) to solve Location-Aware Dispersion.

If unknown nn but kk is known, robots can still detect a rooted configuration. They execute the rooted algorithm using exponential guessing of nn, as described in Section 4.
The remaining configurations, where neither nn nor the configuration type is known, remains as an open problem.
Recall that, no initial configuration (known or unknown) as well as known/unknown n,kn,k denied solution for Dispersion.

Location-Aware Dispersion can be solved deterministically on an arbitrary graph GG with k≤nk\leq n robots, where the initial configuration is unknown but the robots have prior knowledge of nn, using O​(M∗+n/k⋅log⁡(k+Δ))O(M^{*}+n/k\cdot\log(k+\Delta)) bits of memory per robot, where M∗M^{*} denotes the memory required to implement a UXS. The time complexity is: (i) O​(n3+n/k⋅m)O(n^{3}+n/k\cdot m) rounds if k≥⌊n/2⌋+1k\geq\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1; (ii) O​(n4​log⁡n+n/k⋅m)O(n^{4}\log n+n/k\cdot m) rounds if k≥⌊n/3⌋+1k\geq\lfloor n/3\rfloor+1; (iii) O~​(n5)\tilde{O}(n^{5}) rounds otherwise.

We prove that Location-Aware Dispersion can be solved deterministically when the robots have prior knowledge of nn, regardless of the initial configuration.

If the initial configuration is rooted and kk is known, the robots immediately execute the rooted algorithm of Section 3, which guarantees correct dispersion.

Otherwise, the robots first apply the deterministic gathering-with-detection algorithm of Molla et al. [4], which works on arbitrary graphs using only the knowledge of nn and universal exploration sequences. Upon termination, all robots are gathered at a single node and can detect this event, thereby creating a rooted configuration.

If the configuration is rooted but kk is unknown, the robots explore the graph to enable correct identification of the rooted configuration. Once rootedness is confirmed and nn is known, they execute the rooted algorithm of Section 3.

If kk is known but nn is unknown, the robots detect rootedness and execute the rooted algorithm using exponential guessing of nn, as described in Section 4. Correctness follows since the guessed value eventually exceeds the true nn.

After a rooted configuration is obtained with a correct value of nn, dispersion is completed by the rooted algorithm, settling exactly one robot at each occupied node.

The memory required per robot is O​(M∗+n/k⋅log⁡(k+Δ))O(M^{*}+n/k\cdot\log(k+\Delta)), where M∗M^{*} is the memory needed to implement a universal exploration sequence. The stated time bounds follow from the complexities of deterministic gathering and rooted dispersion in the respective cases.

Hence, Location-Aware Dispersion can be solved deterministically on an arbitrary graph with unknown initial configuration when nn is known.
∎

In this work, we studied the Location-Aware Dispersion problem under rooted, dispersed, and general configurations, considering different assumptions on the robots’ prior knowledge of nn and kk. The results are summarized in Table 1.

We also examined the more challenging setting in which the initial configuration is unknown. When robots know kk, they can determine whether the configuration is rooted. However, in the absence of a rooted configuration or without knowledge of kk, a single robot cannot distinguish between dispersed and general configurations, resulting in several open cases for unknown initial configurations. Furthermore, once a dispersed configuration is achieved, the Location-Aware Dispersion problem becomes solvable for both rooted and general configurations. These findings highlight the intrinsic connection between configuration identification, graph exploration, and the solvability of colorful dispersion.

An important direction for future work is to resolve the remaining open cases by identifying minimal additional assumptions, such as limited node memory, partial knowledge of graph parameters, or the availability of additional robots, that enable configuration identification and graph exploration. Another important direction is to see whether time and/or memory complexities of our proposed algorithms could be improved to match the respective time/memory lower bounds. Closing these gaps, as well as extending our results to randomized or fault-tolerant settings, constitute natural avenues for future research.
